ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The mandible is the lower jawbone, forming the oral cavity floor and supporting teeth. It provides attachment for muscles of mastication and is a key landmark for facial symmetry and airway management.

sections.p: The mandible is the only movable bone of the skull, articulating with the temporal bones at the temporomandibular joints (TMJ). It houses the lower teeth and supports the lower face.
b: Single bone, U‑shaped, with a horizontal body and two vertical rami

sections.p: It sits below the maxilla, forming the chin (mental protuberance) and the lower border of the face. The body contains the mandibular canal, the ramus extends upward, and the condyle articulates with the temporal bone.
b: Body: horizontal, contains mandibular foramen and canal; Ramus: vertical, gives rise to coronoid and condylar processes; Condyle: articulates with TMJ

sections.p: Anteriorly, the mental foramen allows passage of mental nerve and vessels. Posteriorly, the mandibular notch separates the condyle from the coronoid process. The inferior alveolar nerve runs within the mandibular canal.
b: Mental foramen: mental nerve, vessels; Mandibular notch: separates condyle and coronoid; Inferior alveolar canal: nerve and artery

sections.p: The mandible receives arterial supply from the inferior alveolar artery (branch of the maxillary artery) and the inferior alveolar branch of the facial artery.
b: Inferior alveolar artery: main supply to body and ramus; Facial artery: supplemental supply to anterior region

sections.p: The inferior alveolar nerve provides sensory innervation to the lower teeth and lower lip, while the mental nerve exits at the mental foramen.
b: Inferior alveolar nerve: sensory to teeth and lower lip; Mental nerve: sensory to chin and lower lip

sections.p: The mandible allows mastication, speech, and provides a framework for facial expression. Its mobility is essential for chewing and swallowing.
b: Mastication: muscle attachments; Speech: articulation; Facial expression: support for muscles

sections.p: Fractures, osteomyelitis, and tumors can affect the mandible. Dental procedures and trauma are common causes of mandibular pathology.
b: Fracture: common in road traffic accidents; Osteomyelitis: infection of bone; Tumors: benign (e.g., odontogenic cyst) or malignant (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma)

sections.p: Remember that the mental foramen is usually located 2–3 mm above the apices of the second premolar. The mandibular canal runs inferior to the molars.
b: Mental foramen location: key landmark for local anesthesia

whenToSeekHelp: Mandibular fracture with swelling or pain, persistent swelling or pus discharge, sudden facial asymmetry, or difficulty breathing

faq.q: What causes a mandibular fracture in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Road traffic accidents, falls, and interpersonal violence are common causes. Lack of protective gear increases risk.

faq.q: How is osteomyelitis of the mandible diagnosed?
faq.a: Clinical signs of pain, swelling, and purulent drainage plus imaging (X‑ray or CT) and positive blood cultures confirm the diagnosis.

faq.q: When is a panoramic X‑ray sufficient for mandibular lesions?
faq.a: For routine dental assessment and simple cysts or fractures; complex lesions or suspected malignancy require CT.
